song.title: Greensleeves: Folk Ballad Fingerstyle
song.summary: This is Greensleeves in A minor, standard tuning, no capo, with the traditional melody played exactly. The key lets open A and E ring under it, and the melody stays on the top three strings in first position until the second verse moves it into barre chords. A lilting 6/8 thumb bass carries it: the thumb plays on beats 1 and 4, the fingers fill the eighths in between, and the melody is pinched on top. Each A-minor phrase ending finishes with a natural-harmonic "bell". The piece builds in steps: a sparse first verse, a refrain that settles into the bass pattern, a second verse in barre chords with a third or sixth under the melody, and a final refrain with a walking bass, a soft thumb slap on beat 4 and the strongest dynamics. It ends on a rolled A minor chord, then the bell rings out.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bar 1 is a slow, free call and answer: open A in the thumb, C and E in the fingers. Bar 2 brings in the bell, the A–E fifth in harmonics that you let ring. Bars 3–4 start the BOOM-chk-chk bass pattern softly (mp) over Fmaj7 and E7, and the bar 4 hammer-on from open G to A (string 3) is the pickup into the verse's Am.

sections.name: A (Verse 1)
sections.note: Keep the verse sparse and quiet (mp). The thumb plays only on beats 1 and 4, and the fingers add a soft inner E or D only while the melody holds a long note, so the tune is always the top voice. The E–F–E hammer/pull in bars 5 and 9 and the G♯→A slide into bar 12 are the only ornaments, and the bell in bar 12 leaves a ringing A–E fifth to lead into the C of the refrain.

sections.name: B (Refrain)
sections.note: The thumb keeps the BOOM-chk-chk pattern going on beats 1 and 4, even under the held G (bars 13 and 17) and the held A (bar 20). The ornaments (the F♯ pull-off, the slide into D, the B–C–B hammer/pull fill in bar 16) should sound like decoration on the melody, not interruptions. The last A minor ends on a single E harmonic, which leads cleanly into Verse 2.

sections.name: A′ (Verse 2)
sections.note: Verse 2 (mf, building through bar 27): the melody stays in the Verse 1 octave but moves into barre shapes, so a third or sixth sits under it on beats 1 and 4. Each bar ends with a bass pickup, ending with the A–B–C climb under G/B and Am/C. The D lands an eighth early, at the end of bars 21 and 25. Bar 21 slides the index from fret 5 to fret 3 on string 2. Bar 25 does the same slide with the middle finger, which leaves the index free for the B bass. Lift each fretted melody note as the next, lower one starts so the tune always stays on top. In bar 28 the bell rings with A doubled on string 6, and a soft B on string 6, fret 7 on the last eighth leads into C without stopping the string 5 harmonic.

sections.name: Climax (Refrain)
sections.note: The bass walks down C–B–A at the start of each four-bar phrase (bars 29–31 and 33–35). Beat 4 is always a light thumb slap with no bass note, and the eighth-note E7 fill in bar 32 (B, G♯, then open E hammered to F♯ and G♯ over a B bass) leads back into the high G. Play forte, ease to mf in bar 35, then let the single 12th-fret harmonic over Am ring into the Outro.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: Bar 37 says "Greensleeves" one last time: C, a pull-off to B, then A over a ringing open-A bass. The C–E rise at the end of the bar rings into the Fmaj7. Hold the tempo through bar 38, then broaden in bars 39–40. Let the A→G♯ pull-off resolve the sus, roll the Am slowly from the bass up, and let the last A harmonic ring under the fermata to pp. Leave a moment of silence before you lift your hands.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the bell
tasteNotes.body: Touch the string directly over the fret wire (fret 7 on string 4, fret 12 on strings 1 and 5) without pressing it down, pick close to the bridge, then lift the finger. Practise the three harmonics slowly over open A until each one rings for the full bar. Fret 7 needs the most precise placement, so check it with a tuner app: the note should be A5.

tasteNotes.title: Lilt comes from beat 1, not speed
tasteNotes.body: 6/8 folk lilt means a heavy pulse on 1, a lighter one on 4, and quiet fill notes. Count '1-2-3-4-5-6' and play the thumb notes at about twice the volume of the fingers. Don't swing the eighths; the hammer-on ornaments give enough sway.

tasteNotes.title: The C–B–A bass walk
tasteNotes.body: In the Climax, G/B links C to Am, so the bass falls stepwise (string 5: frets 3, 2, open) while the melody climbs to G5. These contrary-moving lines are what make the refrain sound fuller without adding notes. Keep your second finger on string 4, fret 2 (E) through all three chords as a common tone where the voicing allows.

tasteNotes.title: Soft slap on beat 4
tasteNotes.body: Let the side of the thumb fall onto strings 5–6 close to the soundhole on beat 4, so they click without ringing. The low-string bass from beat 1 is cut off, but the melody on the treble strings keeps ringing. Use it only in the Climax so it feels like a change of gear.

tasteNotes.title: Build the second verse in layers
tasteNotes.body: For A′, first play only bass and melody in the barre shapes, then add the third or sixth on beats 1 and 4, and last add the beat-6 pickup bass notes. If a barre gets tiring, play the inner voice as a two-string partial barre.

tasteNotes.title: Reference recordings
tasteNotes.body: Listen to John Renbourn and Davey Graham for the English folk-baroque feel in 6/8. Chet Atkins's Greensleeves arrangements show how a thumb bass can carry a lyrical melody. Tommy Emmanuel's ballads show phrase-end harmonics and dynamic building.

song.title: Glasshouse Groove
song.summary: An original percussive pop fingerstyle piece in drop‑D. The low D string drones as a kick‑drum bass while the thumb slaps a snare backbeat on 2 and 4, and a chiming natural‑harmonic hook (F#–D–A–B, played at the 7th and 12th frets) acts as the chorus. It moves from a sparse groove to a fuller second verse, a contrasting B section built on the IV chord with a borrowed bVI colour, and then a climax that brings back the hook over full slap‑and‑knock drums with a 32nd‑note fill. It ends on a strummed D chord and a ringing harmonic chord. Light reharmonization only: sus4 dominants, maj7 colours and one borrowed Bbmaj7.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–2 play the 'glass' hook as natural harmonics over the knock-and-slap cell, with the low D drone left ringing underneath. Bar 2 answers with a G4+B4 harmonic pair that hints at the Gmaj7 coming in bar 3. Bars 3–4 switch to fretted shapes and play each chord change an 8th early. The A7sus4 bar ends with a string-3 2h4 hammer over a C# (string 2, fret 2), then an 8th rest so that C#→D and B→A resolve into the A section's D.

sections.name: A
sections.note: The fretted melody (F#–E–D–E–F#–A) sits over the knock/slap groove, and every chord change is anticipated on the 'and' of 4 by the melody note: A4 into Bm7, G4 into Gmaj7 and Em7, E4 into A7sus4. Bar 5 brings the glass harmonic hook back to open the second phrase, and the A–G–F# pull-off triplet in bar 8 lands on F#, the melody's starting note for A′.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: Every phrase starts on the 'and' of 4 of the bar before. The muted thumb ghost on the 'e' of 3 makes the groove feel busier. Bar 5 plays the glass hook as fretted notes an octave lower (F#–D–A–B, answered by open G+B on beat 4). Bar 8 slides up string 3 into C#, the 3rd of A7, to push hard into B's Gmaj7.

sections.name: B
sections.note: B is where the piece takes a breath. The only drum hit is a slap on beat 4, so let every note ring: open B and E sit in unison with fretted B3 and E4 to make the campanella shimmer, and the G4+B4 harmonics at the end of bar 4 echo the hook's answer. Bar 7's low Bb (string 6, 8th fret) keeps the A4 melody note from bar 6 as a common tone. Bar 8 is the opposite: open A7sus4 chops with 16th slaps that grow into a full strum, ending on G (the 7th) to push into the D climax.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: The hook comes back in full in bars 1 and 5, and its held B4 is now a harp harmonic (fret string 3 at fret 4, touch fret 16, pluck). Under it the thumb plays 16ths that never stop, with knocks on beat 1 and the 'and' of 2. In hook bars the second knock moves one 16th later, to the 'a' of 2, so your right hand is free for the harmonic. The melody is the A melody up the octave. Let the hammer-ons and pull-offs fall on the slaps and knocks. The tapped fill in bar 4 and the 32nd-note run from G5 down to C#5 in bar 8 are the two big moments. Bar 8 ends with tenths stepping down by half steps (A/C#, then G#/C) into the G and B of the Outro's Gmaj7.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: The hook plays one last time over a low G, and its held B4 becomes a harp harmonic (fret string 3 at 4 and touch fret 16). Slaps now land only on beat 3, which slows the cadence. A quick D-shape rasgueado flick on the 'and' of 4 in bar 38 sets up the full drop‑D strum. The piece ends on a 12th‑fret harmonic chime over low D, and a final slap on beat 4 mutes the bass as the last hit.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap goes
tasteNotes.body: Slap on beats 2 and 4 with the side of the thumb landing across strings 5–6 near the end of the fretboard, then bounce off straight away. Never pluck strings 5 or 6 on those beats. The 16th low‑D pickup on the 'a' of 2 is what makes the groove sound 'pop': it pushes beat 3 like a kick drum. Do the body knock on beat 1 with the heel of the palm or the middle finger just below the bridge.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the harmonic hook
tasteNotes.body: Learn the four harmonics as a chord map first: 7th fret on strings 2, 3 and 4, then 12th fret on string 2. Touch the string exactly above the fret wire, pluck near the bridge, and lift the finger as soon as you pluck. Practise the hook with a metronome at 70 BPM with only the beat‑2 slap, then add the knock, then the drone. Let the B4 ring through the beat‑4 slap.

tasteNotes.title: Drop‑D keeps the bass moving smoothly
tasteNotes.body: With low D as a drone, every chord change in A and A′ only moves the upper voices: D to Bm7 to Gmaj7 to A7sus4 shares the A or D on top. The sus4 to 3 resolution (D to C#) is saved for A′ bar 8 and Climax bar 8, so the full A7 sounds like a release. In B, Bbmaj7 slides down a half step to A7sus4 on string 6 (8th fret to 7th fret).

tasteNotes.title: Dynamic arc
tasteNotes.body: Think of the dynamics as one fifth of the performance. Intro: sparse, about mf. A: steady. A′: busier with ghost notes. B: pull back to mp with open strings ringing and half‑time drums. Climax: everything at once. Outro: one big strum, then the harmonics ring out. When you film it, the dynamic changes between sections are what keep viewers watching.

tasteNotes.title: Reference listening
tasteNotes.body: For slap placement and hook‑driven pop arrangements, listen to Sungha Jung's pop covers. For drop‑D harmonics used as a melodic hook, listen to Mike Dawes's 'Somebody That I Used to Know'. For a groove made of a kick knock plus a 16th bass pickup, listen to Kent Nishimura's arrangements. For tapped fills and dynamic builds, listen to Marcin's 'Kashmir'.

song.title: Für Elise: Neo-Soul Groove
song.summary: Beethoven's A-section theme, with every melody pitch kept, set in a laid-back 12/8 neo-soul pocket. Each original 3/8 bar becomes half of a 12/8 bar, so the famous sixteenths turn into lazy triplet eighths at 66 dotted-quarter bpm. That gives a natural Dilla-style lilt, and the fastest picked notes stay plain eighths. The harmony is lightly reharmonized with 9th chords (Am9, E9, Fmaj9, Dm9, E7b9), and the open A and E strings act as the bass. The piece rises from a sparse, open-position first statement to a fuller A′ with new chords, then a relative-major B groove built on the E–D# motif. It peaks in a climax that moves the theme up an octave to 5th–12th position. It ends on a ringing harmonic chime.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Intro (bars 1–4): the groove cell on its own. Keep everything very soft: the body knock is a feather tap, the slaps are barely there, and each shell has a 16th-note hammer-on from the 9th to the 3rd (B→C on string 3 fret 4→5 in Am9, G→A on string 3 open→2 in Fmaj9, E→F on string 4 fret 2→3 in Dm9). In bar 4, Bm7b5 and E7b9 get one pulse each. Pulse 3 then resolves to open A under the rising halo harmonics (G–B–E). The pickup is open e on eighth 11 and string 2 fret 4 on eighth 12, which sets up the Am9 entry of the theme. Bar 4 adds a short Am9 (pulses 3–4) to the planned chords so the halo sounds over the open A bass, as the hook requires. Bar 1 has no slide, so the slide into the E9 3rd waits for its first E9 in the A section.

sections.name: A
sections.note: Section A states the theme twice in the low octave. Each 12/8 bar holds two of Beethoven's bars, with his 16ths written as 8ths. Slaps stay soft. Where the thumb needs the A string for the C–E–A arpeggio, the pulse-4 slap drops out, and it also drops out in bars 4 and 8 so the 12th-fret Am9 halo rings over the open A before the E–D# pickup. Listen for the single B→C hammer-on into the m.4 C in each half (bars 6 and 14 of the piece, i.e. bars 2 and 6 here).

sections.name: A′
sections.note: A′ keeps the theme in the same low open-position octave as A. What changes is the inner voices: a slid shell sits under the melody on eighth 3 or 9 of every bar (in bars 4 and 8, eighth 9 belongs to the halo), and the chords get recoloured. The m.5 phrase now sits over Fmaj9, so its B becomes a #11. The second m.6 goes to Dm9, where an E→F slide on string 4 brings in the 3rd. Over E7b9, the melody's C works as a b13 passing note and pulls off to B. At each cadence, give the A on string 4, fret 7 some vibrato and let the open-A bass carry it under the 12th-fret halo. Bar 4 ends with the E–D# pickup. Bar 8 ends with a G–F–E bass walk on string 6 (pulling off to the open E), which leads up a half-step into the F of section B. In bars 1, 3 and 5, the thumb doesn't slap on pulse 4. Instead the left hand hammers the C on string 5, fret 3 from the ringing open A and takes the backbeat's place. Slap a little harder than in A everywhere else.

sections.name: B
sections.note: Each bar starts with a "call": a chord tone that pulls off a half step and hammers back (A–G#–A, B–A#–B, G–F#–G, C–B–C). A lower chord-tone line answers it. The bass for the next chord comes in on eighth 12, so every change lands early. The knock on eighth 1 then sounds without a bass note under it. In bar 7, the riff comes back to Beethoven's own fingering, open e and string 2 fret 4. Bar 8 climbs E–G#–B and slides from fret 7 to fret 12 on string 1 into the Climax's high E.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: The theme is up in Beethoven's own octave on string 1, while the open A and E bass strings, the 3rd/7th shells and the loudest slaps keep the groove going underneath. Watch for two things: every E–D# figure opens with a quick 32nd-note E–D#–E hammer-pull turn, and the arpeggios slide between the 5th and 7th–8th positions (A→B, B→C) so the melody stays smooth across the position shifts.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: The Outro drops from the Climax's high octave down to open e, and the E–D# motif fades over Fmaj9 before falling E–C–A onto the 3rd of the chord. The Dm9 to E7b9 cadence has no slaps, and its E–D# pickup leads into a last statement of the theme ending on a long, vibratoed A. For the ending, roll the x0-5-5-5-7 Am9 slowly with your thumb from the open A. Then chime the G–B–E halo as an eighth-note triplet over the re-struck A, and make the final slap a palm-muffled thud so the harmonics keep ringing.

tasteNotes.title: Why 12/8 makes Für Elise sound like neo-soul
tasteNotes.body: Beethoven wrote the theme in sixteenths in 3/8. Here each group of 6 sixteenths becomes 6 eighths, which is half of a 12/8 bar. The melody and its rhythm keep the same shape, but every note now sits on a lazy triplet subdivision, the same 'drunk' swing heard on D'Angelo's Voodoo. Count it as four slow pulses, not twelve. The slaps on pulses 2 and 4 give you the backbeat.

tasteNotes.title: Soft slaps, not loud ones
tasteNotes.body: This is lo-fi, so the slap should sound like a brushed snare rather than a crack. Drop the side of your thumb onto strings 5–6 from about 1 cm and let it stay there so it mutes them. Because it mutes the bass, never pluck strings 5–6 on eighths 4 and 10. Put the bass on 1, 7 and the ghost note on 12. Only in the Climax should you let the slap be a little louder.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the Am9 halo
tasteNotes.body: Lightly touch strings 3, 2, 1 directly above the 12th fret wire, pick each one, and lift the finger at once. Play them as a rising triplet while the open A rings. Practise the move from the cadence A (string 3 fret 2 in the low octave, string 1 fret 5 up high) to the harmonics. The halo is only 'touch-pluck-lift', and you must still get to the pickup E–D# on time. Use a metronome at 50 until the pickup never rushes.

tasteNotes.title: The 9→b3 hammer that keeps it jazzy
tasteNotes.body: Inside Am9, the best ornament is the open B string hammered to C at fret 1. It's a 16th-note grace note, which is allowed because it isn't picked. It plays the 9th moving into the minor 3rd, which is the signature move in neo-soul minor chords. Over E9, do the same thing with a slide from F# to G# into the 3rd. Use these in the inner voice only, never at the moment a melody note starts, so the theme stays on top.

tasteNotes.title: Let the reharm hold the melody's 'wrong' notes
tasteNotes.body: In A′ and the Climax, Fmaj9 under 'E D# E B D C' turns the E into the major 7th and the D# into a chromatic lower neighbor. Dm9 under 'A C E A' makes the C a b7, which sounds warm. E7b9 under 'E C B' turns Beethoven's C into a b13 tension. Don't change any melody pitch to fit the chord. The reharmonization works because the chords move and the melody stays the same.

tasteNotes.title: Reference listening
tasteNotes.body: For the pocket, listen to D'Angelo, 'Untitled (How Does It Feel)' and 'Spanish Joint'. For neo-soul chord colors on solo guitar, listen to Isaiah Sharkey, and to Melanie Faye's chord-melody clips. For soft-slap fingerstyle grooves, listen to Kent Nishimura's lo-fi covers and Sungha Jung's slower arrangements. Then listen to a straight piano recording of Für Elise so you know the exact melody you're keeping.

song.title: Gymnopédie No. 1: Ambient Dreamy Fingerstyle
song.summary: Melody not recalled in full: I'm only sure of Satie's opening phrase (F#–A–G–F#–C#–B–C#–D, falling to a long A, then F#). Check the later phrases and the middle-section harmony against the score, or import a file, before tabbing them. The arrangement stays in Satie's D major and uses drop-D tuning, so the low open D and the G at the 5th fret give the famous Gmaj7–Dmaj7 sway a deep bass. Above that bass, the let-ring rootless triads (F#-B-D and F#-A-C#) shimmer on open strings. Every phrase ends with the same "harp chime" of 12th-fret harmonics, which works like a sigh. The texture grows from a bare vamp, to the melody alone in low register, to the melody with filled-in inner voices, to a contrasting middle section, to an octave-up climax with harmonics. A long ringing final chord closes the piece.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Intro (bars 1–4, pp): the "Satie sway" on its own. The thumb rocks between the low G (6th string, 5th fret) and the open drop-D string like a pendulum, and the rootless triads float on beat 2 and ring to the barline. Bar 4 swaps the triad for the harp chime: three 12th-fret harmonics (D-G-B) over the open low D, then the 7th-fret D harmonic on beat 3. Those harmonics spell Gmaj7 over the D bass, so the ear is already pulled toward the Gmaj7 that starts section A.

sections.name: A
sections.note: The melody hangs off the top of the groove cell. Its F# is the top note of both upper triads, so in bars 10–12 the sway itself keeps the long F# ringing. In bar 8 and bar 14 the triad drops out and only the bass and the melody note ring, with vibrato. The section closes with the harp chime over a low D, which sets up the G bass of A′.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: A′ uses the same melody as A at mp, but beat 3 now splits into two 8th-note arpeggio notes, and inside Gmaj7 string 3 hammers from fret 2 to fret 4. The low G (bar 20) and low E (bar 24) arrive an 8th early, and the last 8th of bar 28 (E on string 5, fret 7) leaves your hand in 7th position for the Em7 that opens B.

sections.name: B
sections.note: B leaves the open-D drone for 5th/4th-string bass in 7th position, with the melody sighing down in 1st-string pull-off pairs (D→C#, B→A, C#→B) until one long slide (fret 7→2) shifts the hand into a 2nd-position Bm7. From there the open E string rings through F#m7 and Em7, and the A7sus4 never resolves; its last 8th, the F# at fret 4 on the low 6th string, steps up into the Climax's G bass.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: Satie's opening phrase comes back at its written pitch: F#5–A5 high on the 1st string, then a slide down into 7th position. Open D-G-B strings ring underneath while the left hand travels, and a soft slap lands on beat 3 of bars 37, 39, 41 and 43. The long A in bar 40 is anticipated as a 5th-fret harmonic so the harp chime can open up above it, and in bar 44 the chime gains a 1st-string harmonic (E) as the melody's last note, which floats down into the Outro's Gmaj7.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: The melody fragment F#–A–G now sounds only as harmonics (F#5 at the 7th-fret natural harmonic on the B string, A5 as a harp harmonic over fret 5, G5 at the 5th-fret natural harmonic on the G string), floating over the bare low-G/low-D pendulum. In bar 47 the Gmaj7 lasts one beat, then the full drop-D Dmaj7 unrolls one 8th note at a time. Keep your index on the 1st-string F# while you play the final 12th-fret chime, so the chord keeps ringing under it until it fades.

tasteNotes.title: Keep the F# as a pivot
tasteNotes.body: Both upper triads share F# on the 1st string, 2nd fret. Keep that finger planted, and the other notes move by a single step: B to A on string 3, D to C# on string 2. That is the whole Satie sway, and holding the common tone is what makes it sound seamless.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the harp chime
tasteNotes.body: Lay the ring finger lightly across strings 4-3-2 directly over the 12th fret wire, pluck with p-i-m, and lift off right after the attack. Then reach to the 7th-fret harmonic on string 3. Practise the change from a fretted Dmaj7 into the chime 20 times at 60 bpm until the harmonics bloom evenly.

tasteNotes.title: Space is the arrangement
tasteNotes.body: Satie marks the piece 'Lent et douloureux' (slow and sorrowful). Don't fill beat 3 in sections A and Outro. Let the decay of each note be part of the music. Only A′ and the Climax add motion.

tasteNotes.title: Balance the melody
tasteNotes.body: Play the triads with soft fingertips and the melody with the a-finger rest stroke, or at least a firmer stroke. Record yourself: the melody must still be the clearest voice when everything is ringing in the climax.

tasteNotes.title: References
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Reinbert de Leeuw's very slow piano recording for pacing. For the guitar sound, listen to how players like Andy McKee and Antoine Dufour use harmonics as gentle colour rather than as a showpiece.

song.title: Canon in D: Campanella Wedding Fingerstyle
song.summary: Pachelbel's eight-chord ground bass (D–A–B–F#–G–D–G–A) stays on the thumb all the way through, in drop-D so the D and A roots ring open and the low G and F# sit within easy reach on the 6th string. The famous violin lines go on top in their usual order: first the long-note line (F#–E–D–C#–B–A–B–C#), then the quarter-note line, then the flowing eighth-note lines. Where possible, the melody is fingered so neighbouring notes fall on different strings, mixing open strings with fretted ones (campanella), so they ring into each other like bells. The piece builds through the variations: bare bass and harmonics at first, then one melody voice, then inner voices, then a higher, fuller climax with soft thumb slaps, and finally a slow cadence with a harmonic chime.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: The Intro states the ground bass D–C#–B–A–G–F#–G–A in thumb half notes. Each chord change gets a harmonic: the 12th-fret D–G–B chime on the opening D, then 7th-fret harmonics that spell the chord (A over A/C#, A+F# over F#m/A, and A–D–F# over D/F#). Take bar 1 freely, then settle into tempo. In bars 3–4, open B and E shimmer on beat 2 and on the back half of beat 4 (bar 3) or beat 4 itself (bar 4). The last eighth of bar 4 is a hammer-on from the open B string to C#, which is the leading tone that resolves into the D where the melody comes in.

sections.name: A
sections.note: Bars 5–8 play the hook in the low octave using the ground-bass cell (bass, inner, melody, inner). Bars 9–12 move the second line, D–C#–B–A–G–F#–G–E, up to the violin octave, with the melody on string 1 and the bass on string 6, both walking down the neck together from 10th position to open position. Listen for the slide into the high D, the 12th-fret chime on that D chord, and the F#–G hammer-on in the last bar.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: A′ is where the melody switches to steady eighth notes, and the guitar should start to ring like a harp. Hold down each fretted note while the next note sounds on a different open string (B, G or E), and let the thumb walk in quarter notes from root to octave or fifth. The C#–B–A pull-off at the end of bars 16 and 20 is the little turn back into D, so play it smoothly and get louder to mf on the way.

sections.name: B
sections.note: B (bars 21–28): the texture thins out. The thumb plays only on beat 1, the melody moves to strings 3–2, and open high E and open B ring above it as a drone. Bars 21–24 should sound sparse and singing, with slides on string 2, the Em7 colour and a vibrato on the held E. In bars 25–28 the line climbs in eighth notes over G/A, then a slide down to C# on the A chord and a 12th-fret harmonic chime (B and E) on beat 4 of bar 28 hand off to the Climax.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: Climax (bars 29–36, play it f): the hook comes back an octave up (F#5 at fret 14 on string 1), so the melody walks down the high E string from fret 14 to fret 5. Under it are 3rds and 6ths, a 12th-fret harmonic chime on each D, an eighth-note bass that rocks between root and octave, and a soft thumb slap on beats 2 and 4. Bars 33–36 turn each hook note into a four-note falling scale run, crossing strings so open E and harmonics ring over the fretted notes. It ends with a 7th-fret D-string harmonic (it sounds an A), then the A–B–A–G#–A turn on string 2 to lead into the Outro's D. Bible conflict: it asks for "an octave higher" and "frets 7–10", which can't both be true. I kept the octave, so the hook starts at fret 14 and only settles around frets 5–10 by bar 31.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: The opening hook comes back one last time. It's squeezed into quarter notes, F#–E–D–C# then B–A–B–C#, and you slow down a little more each bar so the C# at the end of bar 38 can linger with vibrato. Bar 39 rolls G and A slowly with the thumb (hold the A under a fermata). Bar 40 rolls the drop-D chord with D on all three low strings and lets it ring, then you lightly touch strings 4–1 at the 12th fret for the final chime while the low D keeps sounding.

tasteNotes.title: Why drop-D works here
tasteNotes.body: Every ground-bass note sits within frets 0–5 on strings 6–5: D open on string 6, A open on string 5, C# at string 5 fret 4, B at string 5 fret 2, F# at string 6 fret 4, G at string 6 fret 5. That leaves your fretting hand free for the melody, and the open low D and A ring under everything. Practise the bass line alone, slowly and evenly, until your thumb can play it without you watching.

tasteNotes.title: The bass line falls by step
tasteNotes.body: The ground bass moves D→C#→B→A→G→F#→G→A. The slash chords (A/C#, F#m/A, D/F#) are what let it walk down by step instead of jumping between roots. Keep the slash bass notes, and don't fall back to root-position A, F#m or D. Those stepwise notes are what make it sound like Pachelbel.

tasteNotes.title: Fingering the campanella
tasteNotes.body: In the eighth-note variations, choose fingerings where neighbouring melody notes sit on different strings. For example, play D on string 2 fret 3, then the next note on an open string, so both ring together. Lift a finger only when the next note needs that string. The overlap is what gives you the harp-like ring that suits a wedding.

tasteNotes.title: Building the dynamics
tasteNotes.body: Plan four dynamic levels: Intro pp, A mp, A′ mf, B dropping back to mp, Climax f, Outro fading out. Record a run-through and check that the climax is clearly the loudest. Keep the slaps on 2 and 4 soft, like a brush on a snare, and never louder than the melody.

tasteNotes.title: Harmonic chimes
tasteNotes.body: Play the 12th-fret harmonics on strings 4–2 together: lay a finger flat over the fret wire, pluck, and lift right away. Practise moving from the last melody note into the harmonic without a gap. That moment marks the start of each new cycle and the final ending.

tasteNotes.title: Listening
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Sungha Jung's and Kent Nishimura's fingerstyle versions of Canon in D for the open-string sound and the slow build. Also listen to a period-instrument recording, such as Musica Antiqua Köln, to hear how the violin lines enter one after another over the ground bass.

song.title: House of the Rising Sun — Dark Arpeggio Blues Fingerstyle
song.summary: A one-guitar showpiece built on the famous 6/8 A-minor arpeggio. The traditional melody (in its familiar Animals-era form) stays on top and isn't changed. The piece starts quiet and moody, with plain open-string arpeggios, a chromatic bass walk (A–G–F#–F) and a harmonic chime. It then moves to a darker interlude on the iv chord (Dm), and finally a percussive last verse with a body knock on beat 1, a thumb slap on beat 4, passing bass notes and a fill at the end of each phrase. It ends on a rasgueado-style Am strum with a final harmonic chime. Everything is in standard tuning with no capo, so the open A, E and high-e strings can drone and keep the sound dark.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: The Chime Rise opens the piece softly. Its slide to the high A and the 12th-fret harmonics should ring into the thumb's chromatic walk down, A–G–F#–E, which falls one step per bar. Bars 2–4 use the bass, 3-2-1-2-3 rocking arpeggio that runs under the whole tune. Let the G# in bar 4 hang with vibrato so it pulls hard toward the Am of the first verse.

sections.name: A — Verse 1
sections.note: This is the quietest statement of the tune. The thumb keeps the plain root-and-5th cell going while the a finger plays each syllable on strings 1–2. From bar 13 the hammer-ons and the F-E and G-E-D# pull-offs build toward the end of the verse, and the harmonic chime on the last eighth of bar 20 carries straight into the Dm interlude.

sections.name: B — Interlude (Dark Contrast)
sections.note: The open A string keeps droning while the left hand moves between the fret-5 Dm barre and the fret-5 Am shape. A long slide up to the D at fret 10 leads into each falling D–C–A phrase, and the line climbs to the F barre at fret 8. Bar 26 ends on the harp harmonic on the low E and a string-1 triplet (open–4–5) that hammers onto A. Bar 27 brings back the Chime Rise with a G–F–E pull-off in the bass. In bar 28 the bass climbs E–F#–G# in 16ths, which pulls straight into the slapped Am at the start of the climax.

sections.name: Climax — Verse 2 (Percussive)
sections.note: Knock and bass on eighth 1, slap on eighth 4 in every bar. The chromatic walk A–G–F#–F (and later G–F#–F–E) moves up string 5 at frets 12–8, and the high-octave melody rides on string 1 above it. Bar 29 restates the Chime Rise. The four fills then grow, from a pull-off run (bar 32) to tapped harmonics (bar 36) to an open-string E–G#–B–E run (bar 40) and a rasgueado (bar 44). Melody note: this is a reconstruction of the vocal's rising and falling contour, written from memory and placed an octave up. Import a melody file if you want the exact sung notes.

sections.name: Outro — Big Ending
sections.note: The energy drops first: bar 45 plays Am at half speed, and bar 46 climbs an Fmaj7 up to the open high E. The ending then builds again: a slap, a body knock and a 16th-note open-string E7 run lead to G# (the leading tone), which resolves up to the high A in the final rasgueado. The fret-12 harmonic chime follows at once, and the low A carries a slow vibrato under both.

tasteNotes.title: The chromatic bass walk is the hidden second hook
tasteNotes.body: Am → C/G → D/F# → F produces a bass line that falls A–G–F#–F while the open B and E strings stay constant above it. It appears in the intro and returns in the climax, so the ear knows the peak is related to the opening. Use your thumb for C/G on string 6 at fret 3 and D/F# on string 6 at fret 2, and keep the upper strings ringing as the bass moves.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap and knock go in 6/8
tasteNotes.body: In 6/8 the backbeat is eighth 4 (the second dotted-quarter beat), not beats 2 and 4. Knock on the body under the soundhole with the side of the thumb on eighth 1 and play the bass on the same eighth. Slap strings 5–6 with the thumb on eighth 4 and don't pluck a bass note there. Practise the climax cell on open Am at 50 bpm until the slap sounds as loud as the melody note.

tasteNotes.title: Practising the Chime Rise harmonics
tasteNotes.body: Lay your ring finger flat across strings 3-2-1 directly over the 12th fret wire, touching the strings without pressing them down, and pluck p-i-m-a together. Lift the finger straight away. If the G string sounds dull, you are slightly on the fret side of the wire, so move toward the bridge. Practise slide (fret 5) → lift → chime until the move takes less than one eighth note.

tasteNotes.title: Keep it dark: avoid bright major sounds
tasteNotes.body: Play the E chord as a plain triad or E7 with the open low E. Don't add a 9th or 13th, because the hard G# leading tone gives the piece its blues-noir sound. In the interlude, let the Dm sit on the open A drone so the minor-6th note (F) clashes against the drone. That clash makes the sound darker than the verse.

tasteNotes.title: Reference recordings
tasteNotes.body: Listen to The Animals (1964) for the 6/8 arpeggio pulse and the organ-solo shape that the interlude follows. Listen to Dave Van Ronk's and Bob Dylan's early recordings for the rawer folk-blues version with the chromatic bass. For the percussive climax, study Mike Dawes and Kent Nishimura, who place slaps in compound time without the melody losing its legato.

song.title: Ode to Joy (Percussive Pop Fingerstyle)
song.summary: Beethoven's theme is moved up a major third to E major and played with a capo at 4, so you finger easy open C-shapes and the open strings ring out. The harmony is reworked as a pop progression: I–IV | V–iii7 | vi–IVmaj7 | I–V, then the same again ending V7–I. That gives the hymn a modern singer-songwriter feel. Your thumb plays the bass on 1 and 3 and slaps the low strings on 2 and 4. Body knocks on the 16th note before beat 3 work as a kick drum, and hammer-ons in the inner voices fill the gaps. Bar 4 ends with a 12th-fret harmonic chime as the hook. The second half gets busier with 16th-note fills, a slide, and a hammer-on landing on a slap. It ends with a run of harp harmonics over the final chord.

sections.name: A: Groove
sections.note: The melody stays on strings 1–2 in open position, and the thumb alternates between bass notes on 1 and 3 and slaps on 2 and 4. Keep this half fairly light so the second half has somewhere to grow. The 12th-fret harmonic chord at the end of bar 4 is the hook.

sections.name: A': Climax & Harp-Harmonic Ending
sections.note: This half uses the same thumb pattern, but the inner voices move in 16ths, the melody slides into G (bar 5), and the D in bar 6 is hammered on at the same moment as the slap. The C chord arrives an 8th early in bar 8. After that, harp harmonics finish the piece.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap goes
tasteNotes.body: On beats 2 and 4, bring the side of your thumb down onto strings 5–6 near the end of the fingerboard so it snaps against the frets like a snare. At the same moment, pluck the melody with i/m. Never pluck strings 5–6 on those beats, because the slap mutes them anyway. On beats 1 and 3, the thumb plays the actual bass note (C, G, E, A, F shapes). Those alternating jobs are the whole groove.

tasteNotes.title: The 12th-fret chime hook (bar 4)
tasteNotes.body: In bar 4, let the D on beat 3 ring with a little vibrato. Then lay your index finger lightly across strings 4–2 directly over the 12th fret (relative to the capo, so fret 16 on the neck). Pluck those strings on the beat-4 slap. You get a G-chord bell that echoes the melody's D. Practise just the move from fret 3 to the harmonics until it lands in time with no gap.

tasteNotes.title: Harp-harmonic ending
tasteNotes.body: In bar 8, hold the C shape. Touch each string 12 frets above its fretted note with your right index finger (string 4 at 14, string 3 at 12, string 2 at 13, string 1 at 12, all relative to the capo). Pluck with your ring finger, one string per 16th note. On the final eighth, your thumb plucks the low C on string 5 at the same moment as the last harmonic on string 2, so the tonic bass sits under the chime.

tasteNotes.title: Pop reharm with inner-voice motion
tasteNotes.body: Instead of the textbook I–V, the melody sits over I–IV | V–iii7 | vi–IVmaj7. In bar 3, the D over the A shape is a 6th, and then the open-E melody note turns it into a full maj7. In bars 2 and 6, the bass walks E–B–A from the iii7 into the vi. The hammer-ons on string 4 (D→E) keep the 16ths moving without crowding the tune.

tasteNotes.title: Build it in layers
tasteNotes.body: Start at 70 bpm with thumb only: bass, slap, bass, slap. Add the melody on top. Then add the body knock on the 16th before beat 3, using the heel of your picking hand on the lower bout. Add the hammer-ons last. In bar 6, the D is hammered on while you slap, so the left hand supplies the note and the right hand supplies the snare. Slow that bar down on its own until the two line up exactly.

tasteNotes.title: Listening
tasteNotes.body: Sungha Jung's pop covers show the same slap-on-2-and-4 groove under a simple melody. Kent Nishimura's arrangements are good for clean harp-harmonic endings, and Mike Dawes's 'Somebody That I Used to Know' cover shows the harmonic tricks pushed further.

song.title: Drunken Sailor: Stomping Shanty Fingerstyle
song.summary: This sets the traditional melody exactly as written, in D Dorian on a drop-D guitar, so the low open D can drone and stomp like a crew's boots on deck. Bass drum and snare come from the guitar body: a knock on beat 1 and a thumb slap on beats 2 and 4. Every two-bar melodic phrase is treated as the call, and the guitar answers it in the gaps with short licks and a three-note harmonic chime at the 12th fret (D–G–B). The chime's natural B is the 6th of D minor, the note that makes the key Dorian, so the guitar's signature sound is also the mode's colour. The form builds from a bare verse to a sparse, singing B section, then to a full chorus climax, and ends on a harmonic chime and a rasgueado-style strum.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–2 are just the stomp: a knock on the low D on 1, slaps on 2 and 4, and a quiet A (string 4, fret 7) on every 'and'. Bar 2 adds the low D on beat 3 and a soft F to give the minor colour, and bar 3 adds the open B string for the Dm6 sound. Bar 4 brings in the hook: a C→D hammer-on on string 5, then the 12th-fret harmonic chord on strings 4-3-2. There's no slap on beat 4 here, so the chime can ring into the Dm of bar 5.

sections.name: A (Verse 1: What shall we do…)
sections.note: The repeated A stays on string 3, fret 2 while the thumb keeps the knock–slap stomp on roots only. Bars 6, 8 and 10 each end with a small answer (open strings, then a pull-off to the open B), and the C-to-A slide on string 3 at "Ear-ly" leads into the first full Dorian chime of the verse in bar 12.

sections.name: A′ (Chorus: Way hay and up she rises)
sections.note: The repeated chorus A moves up an octave to string 1, fret 5 so the 'Way hay' sounds like a shout. The thumb anticipates each new bass note on the "and" of 4, and in bar 18 it walks D–C–B–A against the rising A–B–C–D melody. Bar 19 uses a pull-off from C to A, and bar 20 ends on the full Dorian chime, left to ring into the quiet B section.

sections.name: B (Verse 2: Put him in the longboat…)
sections.note: The slaps stop here. Your thumb plays each repeated-note call alone on string 4 (A at fret 7, then G at fret 5 over a low C), and your fingers answer an octave higher with "sai-lor". Each answer ends on a single 12th-fret harmonic over a soft knock: A, then D, then B over G/D for the bright Dorian sound, then D again. In the last line the roles swap: your fingers sing "Ear-ly in the" up high, your thumb answers "morn-ing" on the low D, and an open-A pickup leads into the climax.

sections.name: Climax (Chorus: Way hay…, full deck)
sections.note: Climax (bars 29–36): the 'Way hay' melody sits high (A on string 1, fret 5; G at fret 3), and each bar starts with a 16th-note slide over a knock and low D. Double-stops sound under the held melody note while the thumb plays steady 8ths, with slaps on 2 and 4. The chime goes off on beats 3–4 of bars 30, 32 and 34; leave the slap off on those beat 4s so the harmonics ring. Bar 36 lands on D and finishes with a D–E–D hammer/pull, then an open A in the bass leads into the Outro's Dm.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: Outro: 'Ear-ly in the morn-ing' (C–A–G–E, then D–D) runs down string 1 with a slide into the A. It keeps the slaps for one last bar, then lets the G/D ring with only knocks, so the line seems to slow down without any change in tempo. The C→D hammer-on on string 5 at the end of bar 38 sets off the held chime in bar 39, a knock on beat 4 takes a breath, and the rasgueado on the drop-D Dm builds to a big chord that the final slap cuts off.

tasteNotes.title: Let the B natural tell you it's Dorian
tasteNotes.body: D natural minor would use B♭; this piece never does. The natural B shows up in Dm6, in G/D and in the D–G–B harmonic chime. Lean on the B in each of those places and the piece sounds old and sea-worn rather than gloomy.

tasteNotes.title: Slap and knock placement
tasteNotes.body: Use the side of your thumb to slap strings 6–4 near the end of the fingerboard on beats 2 and 4, and keep your fingers free to pluck melody on top. For the knock on beat 1, tap the upper bout with the heel of your palm or the fingertips of your picking hand, and sound the low D with your thumb on the same beat. Never pluck string 6 on a slap beat.

tasteNotes.title: Drilling the chime
tasteNotes.body: Lay your fret-hand ring finger lightly over strings 4–2 exactly above the 12th fret wire, pluck with p-i-m together, and lift the finger right away. Loop the last two bars of the Intro slowly (about 70 bpm) until the C→D hammer-on (string 5, fret 3→5) flows straight into the chime without a gap. Then bring it up to 104.

tasteNotes.title: Walk the bass, anticipate the change
tasteNotes.body: In A′ and the climax, land the new bass note an 8th early: on the 'and' of 4, before C, Am or C/E arrives. The stepwise line D–C–B–A gives the stomp a push forward. Keep the melody finger anchored on the shared notes (A, then G) so only the bass moves.

tasteNotes.title: Reference sounds
tasteNotes.body: Listen to The Longest Johns' versions of shanties for phrasing and how call-and-response works. Listen to Kent Nishimura and Sungha Jung for how they balance slaps with a singing top line. Listen to Tommy Emmanuel for harmonic chimes used as punctuation rather than decoration.

song.title: Scarborough Fair — DADGAD Harp & Drone Setting
song.summary: This is a solo setting of Scarborough Fair in DADGAD, in D Dorian. The melody follows the familiar traditional/Simon & Garfunkel contour (Are you going to Scarborough Fair = D D A A E F E D), but it is not a note-for-note copy of any recording. The open D, A and D strings drone under every bar. The 3/4 lilt stays harp-like, and the piece builds like a story. The Intro sets out the hook: the first four melody notes played as ringing cross-string notes and capped by harp harmonics. Verse A is sparse, with only a bass note and the melody. B drops the melody into the thumb register under a high open-string drone so the second half of the tune sounds new. The Climax brings back the full verse with campanella runs, harp-harmonic answers at each phrase end and a fuller bass. The Outro repeats the hook as a harmonic chime and ends on a slow rolled strum of the whole open tuning.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: The Scarborough chime (D–A–E–F) is played across different strings over a low-D bass, so each note keeps ringing into the next. Two harp harmonics (A, D) answer it. In bars 3–4 the C/D keeps the open D and A strings sounding, so it sounds like a Dorian drone rather than a real chord change. Hold the final D in bar 4 as a breath before the verse.

sections.name: A — Verse 1
sections.note: This verse is just the tune over a single bass note in each bar, so let the DADGAD open strings ring under it. The G-major bar (bar 11) brings in the Dorian B♮ with a hammer-on on 'rose-ma-ry'. The verse ends with the Scarborough chime and two harp harmonics answering 'true love of mine'.

sections.name: B — Low Verse (contrast)
sections.note: The thumb plays the second half of the tune ('Remember me… true love of mine') on the 4th string, sliding down the neck from fret 12 to the open string like a cello line. Meanwhile i and m keep an unbroken eighth-note drone on the open A and D strings. Start at p and swell from bar 25, where the thumb sweeps across the open D–A–D bass strings. Bar 28 lands on 'mine' and climbs out through the G–A–B♮ hammer triplet to the open high D, ready for the Climax.

sections.name: Climax — Verse 2
sections.note: The melody moves up to strings 1–2 (D4–D5) over the full harp-lilt cell: bass on 1, open-4th drone on the & of 1, open-A fills, with a bass pickup on beat 3 into each new phrase. Listen for the harp-harmonic echoes after each phrase-end note and the campanella runs in bars 36, 40 and 44. Bar 44 gives you a full Dm strum and then the hook as harmonics (D–A–E–F). Its campanella run lands on A3, which leads into the Outro chime.

sections.name: Outro — Chime & Strum
sections.note: Slow down a little more in each bar. The 12th-fret chime in bar 45 and the 7th-fret C/D chime in bar 46 hint at the ♭VII over the low D drone that never stops. The Dm roll in bar 47 is played as single 16ths from low to high and left to ring, and the piece ends on a 12th-fret harmonic chord with F on the 5th string at fret 8 for the minor colour. Hold that last chord until it fades out.

tasteNotes.title: Dorian lives in the G-major chord
tasteNotes.body: In D Dorian the B♮ is the one note that separates the tune from plain D minor. Give it room in bar 7 of each verse ('…mary and thyme'). Fret the low G on the 6th string at fret 5 and let the melody's B ring against the open D drones. If that bar sounds bright and slightly unexpected, you're doing it right. Don't change it to B♭.

tasteNotes.title: Harp harmonics, practised in slow motion
tasteNotes.body: Lightly touch the string 12 frets above the fretted (or open) note with the right-hand index finger, then pluck behind it with the ring finger (a). Thumb and fretting hand keep the drone going. First practise the two-note answer in the hook alone: 1st string open (touch at fret 12) and 2nd string fret 7 (touch at fret 19). Use a metronome at 60 and play them as two quarter notes. Then alternate them with regular plucked notes so you get the harp effect where harmonics and normal notes ring together.

tasteNotes.title: Campanella = no two neighbouring notes on the same string
tasteNotes.body: For the 16th-note runs in the Climax, finger each scale step on a different string. For example, D (1st string, open), C (2nd string, fret 3), B♮ (3rd string, fret 4), A (2nd string, open), G (3rd string, open), F (4th string, fret 3), E (4th string, fret 2). Every note overlaps the next and the run sounds like a harp glissando. Plan these fingerings before you add speed.

tasteNotes.title: Shape the dynamic arc on purpose
tasteNotes.body: Record the whole piece and check that it matches this curve: Intro mp, A mp with only the bass and melody, B p (the deepest dip), Climax growing to f at bar 44, then the Outro chiming quietly before the final strum, which should be the loudest single gesture. On camera the B section's restraint is what makes the Climax hit.

tasteNotes.title: Reference players
tasteNotes.body: Pierre Bensusan for DADGAD drones and modal phrasing. Tony McManus ('Ceol More') for Celtic ornaments and harp-like campanella. Martin Simpson's traditional English settings for how to let a ballad melody breathe over open strings. Also Simon & Garfunkel's 'Scarborough Fair/Canticle' for the vocal phrasing and lilt. The melody here follows the familiar contour but makes no claim to note-for-note accuracy.

song.title: Danny Boy (Londonderry Air): Celtic Ballad Fingerstyle
song.summary: The traditional Londonderry Air melody is kept note-for-note in D major, played in DADGAD so the open D and A strings drone under the melody like uilleann pipes. The piece starts as a bare, singing line over a low D pedal. It thickens through A′ and the bridge, then peaks in a high, ringing climax with chiming harmonics before ending on a harmonic chord that rings out. Each long melody note is reached with a slide and held with vibrato, so the guitar phrases like a singer taking breaths.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–2 set up the drone. The low D and the open DADGAD strings ring while the G-to-A hammer-on and the F# on fret 4 change Dsus4 into D. Bar 3 is the "chiming D" hook: fret-12 harmonics, then fret-7 harmonics, then a slide from A to B on string 1. In bar 4 the D on top of Asus4 resolves to C# on the last pickup note, so the pickup notes A–B–C# lead straight into 'Oh Danny boy'.

sections.name: A
sections.note: The A section has a sparse texture. The thumb plays only on beats 1 and 3, so the melody on strings 1–2 sounds like a singer over a pipe drone. Grace-note slides from two frets below lead into 'pipes', 'call-ing', 'glen' and 'side'. Bar 12 stops on the A7 half cadence with only bass and melody, then the A–B–C# hammer pickup leads back to D.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: A′ uses the same melody as A, but the full pipe-drone cell now fills every off-beat with open G/D/A strings. Listen for the quick hammer/pull turns on "ro-ses" (string 1, frets 2-4-2, then a pull to the open D) and "fall-ing" (string 2, frets 2-4-2-0). In bar 16 the E7 arrives an 8th early, under a G# with vibrato. Bar 20 settles on D and then rings the chiming-D harmonics (fret 12 on strings 4-3-2, then fret 7 on strings 2-1). The pickup "But come ye" goes up string 1 (fret 7, slide to 9, then 11) to lead into the G of the bridge.

sections.name: B
sections.note: I wrote this bridge melody from memory of how it's usually sung, so check it against a recording you trust. In B the bass stops droning and moves: G–F#–G–F# under the first line, then D–C#–B into the F#m. Open G, D and A strings chime between the melody notes, and the melody climbs to the B on 'hushed' (1st string, fret 9) and then to the G–E7 shape around frets 7–10. Start quietly and get gradually louder until bar 28. There, 'snow' slides down onto Asus4, and the pickup A–B–C# into the Climax is a hammer-on and slide up the 2nd string, not the 1st.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: The climax keeps the drone pulse going but makes it fuller. The melody doubles in octaves at the same fret on strings 4+1 or 5+2, a soft slap falls on beat 4 of bars 30, 32 and 34, and the chiming-D harmonics ring on 'Oh Dan-ny boy' (bar 33) before the slide lands on B. The emotional peak is the octave B falling to B♭ in bar 35 (G to Gm). After it, the bar-36 pull-off run ends on C# so the Outro's D resolves.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: Outro: the last 'so' slides up the 1st string from fret 10 to the high D at fret 12 over a pipe-drone tail. The echo 'Oh Dan-ny' is played an octave lower over Gmaj7/D, using hammer-ons on the 2nd string. The open Dsus4 roll then supplies the open top D as the echo's 'boy'. In the last bar, the fret-12 harmonic chime is followed by a fret-4 harmonic on string 4 (F#), which turns the open-string sus sound into a true D major before the low D rings out.

tasteNotes.title: Slide like a singer
tasteNotes.body: Slide into the long notes ('pipes', 'call-', 'side', 'so') from two frets below, starting the slide ON the beat so the target note is slightly late. That small delay makes it sound sung. Add vibrato only after the note has sounded for a beat.

tasteNotes.title: The harmonic chime hook
tasteNotes.body: Lay your ring finger lightly across strings 4-3-2 directly over the 12th fret wire and pluck p-i-m together, then lift. Next, touch strings 2-1 over fret 7 and pluck a-m. Practise it as a 2-beat move until the bass D under it never stops ringing.

tasteNotes.title: Let the drones do the harmony
tasteNotes.body: In DADGAD the open D-A-D-A strings already form the D chord, so G, Bm and E7 need only one or two fretted notes against them. Keep fretted notes minimal so the open strings ring through the changes like pipe drones.

tasteNotes.title: Minor iv for 'I love you so'
tasteNotes.body: The only real reharmonization is G to Gm under 'love you'. The Bb in Gm against the melody falls by a half step to A on D/A. Lean into it with a slight slowdown: it is the emotional peak of the piece.

tasteNotes.title: Rubato within a steady pulse
tasteNotes.body: Learn every section strictly at 60 bpm with a metronome. Then take time only at phrase ends (bars 4 and 8 of each section) and return to tempo on the next pickup. The pickup notes always sound in time.

tasteNotes.title: Reference recordings
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Pierre Bensusan's DADGAD playing for the drone sound, Tony McManus's Celtic air arrangements for ornament placement, and Eva Cassidy's 'Danny Boy' for phrasing and breath on the long notes.

song.title: Amazing Grace — Sunday Night Sway (Gospel Neo-Soul Chord-Melody)
song.summary: This plays Amazing Grace in D with the melody exactly as the hymn goes. It is tuned to drop D so a low open D can ring under every phrase like a church organ pedal. The piece is 40 bars and follows the hymn's 16-bar verse: the first half is A, the second half is A′, B brings back the first half an octave higher over minor chords, and the Climax brings back the second half with the fullest playing. The hymn's simple three chords are swapped for lush 9th and 13th chords (maj9, m9, 13sus4) and church-style moves like Gm6 to Dmaj9 (the "Amen" sound). The arc is: soft opening, a gentle swaying verse, a darker middle, a full gospel climax, and a ringing harmonic ending. A short 'Grace Lick' (a slide into the melody, a hammer-on and a harmonic) closes every section and ties the piece together.

sections.name: Intro
sections.note: Bars 1–3 sit over the open low D (drop-D) while the top voice walks down F#–E–D. Each bar's small hammer-on adds the neo-soul 9th-to-3rd colour. Bar 4 ends the walk on C#: the dyad slides into the D of A13sus4, then pulls off to B and hammers to C# for A13. The fret-12 harmonics chime, and the pickup A (string 3, fret 2) on beat 3 leads into Dmaj9.

sections.name: A
sections.note: Keep it sparse and singing at mp. Each bar has just the thumb bass on 1 and a soft pinch on 2, with no hammer-ons yet, and the long notes slide in from a fret below: 'grace' (F#), 'sound' (A, with the bass on string 5) and 'me' (A). Bar 8 plays the Grace Lick over A: the F#+A dyad slides from 6/4 to 7/5, then string 3 hammers from 4 to 6 (B to C#, the 9th rising to the 3rd), the fret-12 chime sounds on the 'and' of 2, and the pickup 'I' (A, string 3 fret 2) lands on beat 3. Damp the chime with your right palm as the pickup sounds so the melody stays on top going into A′.

sections.name: A′
sections.note: The Sway Cell now plays in full: listen for the E→F# hammer-on on string 4 on the 'and' of 2, and for the chromatic line B→B♭→A on string 3 that takes 'now am found' through Gm6 into Dmaj9/A. The section ends with an 'Amen' (Gm6/D), the Grace Lick climbing up the neck to D–G–B harmonics at fret 12, and a pickup A on string 2, fret 10, which puts your hand in place for the B section's high melody.

sections.name: B
sections.note: Section B sets "Amazing grace… like me" an octave up on the top string, with D5 at fret 10, F#5 at 14 and A5 at 17. Under it, the bass walks down B–A–G–F#, so the hymn's tonic notes turn into the dark 3rd and 5th of Bm9, and the A in bar 4 becomes the gritty #9 of F#7#9. Bars 2 and 6 change chord on the 'and' of 3. Bar 6 also changes tone colour: F#5 is a harp harmonic and E5 a natural harmonic over open-string Em11. Bar 7 holds the high A with vibrato. Bar 8 plays the Grace Lick quietly over an open A bass instead of the low D drone. On beat 3 it drops to A7b9, with F#4 on top as the pickup on "I" leading into the Climax's Dmaj9.

sections.name: Climax
sections.note: Each downbeat is a fast thumb-to-index roll of a 4–5-note grip, with a hammer on the 'and' of 2 (9th to 3rd: E–F# in bars 1, 4 and 5, A–B in bar 2, C–C# in A13) and a thumb ghost on the 'and' of 3. Listen for the half-step inner moves (D#→D into Em9, B♭→A in the A7b9 pull-off) and for bar 7's hammer-on run, which carries 'see' from D4 up to D5. To make room for the grips, 'am' is shortened to an eighth note so Gm6 can enter, and 'found/was' moves up an octave to A4.

sections.name: Outro
sections.note: Outro, bars 37–40, played slower and slower: the last 'now I see' (F#–E–D) is played in harmonics: string 2 at fret 7, string 1 at fret 12, then string 4 at fret 5. Under them, the E→F# hammer-on and then a B♭→A pull-off over Gm6/D give the plagal 'Amen'. After a slow rolled Dmaj9 up to a high F# with vibrato, the Grace Lick gets one last stretched-out play: slide the F#+B dyad from frets 6 to 7, hammer E to F# on string 3 (frets 9 to 11), then strike the fret-12 chime on strings 1–3 with the open low D and let it all fade to silence.

tasteNotes.title: Gm6 → Dmaj9: the half-step 'Amen'
tasteNotes.body: The church sound in the A′ and Climax cadences comes from one inner voice: B-flat (the minor 3rd of Gm6) falls to A (the 5th of D). At the same time E holds over as the 9th, and G falls to F#. Keep your fingers as close as possible here and only move the notes that change. The low D drone means the bass never moves, so all the emotion sits in that half step.

tasteNotes.title: Slides that sing, not smear
tasteNotes.body: Slide into melody notes from exactly one fret below, starting slightly before the beat so the target lands on the beat. Only the A section's long notes ('grace', 'sound', 'me') get slides. If every note slides, none of them stand out. Keep pressure light during the slide and press down firmly on arrival.

tasteNotes.title: The 9-to-3 hammer is the neo-soul fingerprint
tasteNotes.body: The E-to-F# hammer-on on string 4 (frets 2 to 4) in the Sway Cell plays the 9th resolving to the 3rd. That is the vocal 'bend' gospel singers use. Hold it back for the whole A section so that when it arrives in A′ it sounds like the choir coming in.

tasteNotes.title: Practise the Grace Lick on its own first
tasteNotes.body: Loop the one-bar Grace Lick at 60 bpm: slide on beat 1, hammer-on on the 'and' of 2, harmonics on beat 3. Play the fret-12 harmonics by lightly touching strings 1–3 directly above the fret wire with one finger flat across them, then lift as you pluck. The low D must keep ringing underneath, so let the thumb rest away from string 6.

tasteNotes.title: Feel 3/4 like a slow 6/8
tasteNotes.body: Count '1-and-2-and-3-and' but lean on beat 1 and let beats 2 and 3 float slightly late. That lazy pull is the sway. Practise with a metronome clicking only on beat 1 at 72 bpm so you learn to place the swing yourself.

tasteNotes.title: Listening
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Cory Henry's organ reharmonizations of hymns for the chord colours. Listen to Isaiah Sharkey and Melanie Faye for neo-soul hammer-on licks on guitar. Listen to Tommy Emmanuel's solo hymn medleys for how to keep a drone bass and melody independent in a chord-melody arrangement.

song.title: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star – Percussive Pop Fingerstyle
song.summary: The nursery rhyme is moved up a major third to E major. This lets the open low E and A strings drive a modern percussive groove: a body knock on beat 1, thumb slaps on 2 and 4, and a busy thumb line under the melody, which always stays on top on the first two strings. Section A keeps the familiar I–IV–V harmony and introduces the signature move, a 12th-fret harmonic chime in the gap after the long note. It ends with an open-string hammer-on run that slides into the second phrase. Section B adds pop colour chords (E/G#, C#m7 with a common-tone move to Amaj7, G#m7), 7th-fret harmonics, a chromatic walk-up in the bass and a triplet roll. It ends on a big Eadd9 strum and a three-string harmonic chime. The melody is exact; the chords are a tasteful reharmonization.

sections.name: A – Groove & Chime
sections.note: Get the knock–slap backbeat steady under a plain melody first. The 12th-fret chime in bar 2 is the hook, and bar 4's open-string hammer-on run (0-2-4 on the high E string) slides straight into bar 5.

sections.name: B – Climax & Chime Ending
sections.note: Fuller texture: more 16th-note motion underneath, colour chords (C#m7 to Amaj7 keeps G# and E on the inner strings), 7th-fret harmonics and a chromatic B–C–C# bass walk-up in bar 6. It ends with a full Eadd9 strum and a harmonic chime on strings 6, 2 and 1.

tasteNotes.title: Knock on 1, slap on 2 and 4
tasteNotes.body: On every beat 1, tap the side of the guitar top near the bridge with the heel of your picking hand while your thumb plucks the bass note. That knock is the kick drum. On beats 2 and 4, bounce the side of your thumb onto strings 6–5 near the end of the fingerboard so they click against the frets. Bass notes are never written on a slap beat, so your thumb is always free for it. Practise bars 1 and 3 with just the knock, the slap and the bass until the backbeat feels automatic, then add the melody.

tasteNotes.title: The harmonic hook (bars 2, 6 and 8)
tasteNotes.body: Each long melody note leaves a gap on beat 4, and that is where the chime goes. In bar 2, lightly touch strings 1–2 right over the 12th fret with your fretting hand while the picking thumb slaps. Then lift your hand straight away so the chime rings. Bar 6 uses the same move at the 7th fret (F#5 and B5 over the B chord). The ending adds string 6 at the 12th fret. Pluck strings 6, 2 and 1 together for an open-fifth E chime.

tasteNotes.title: Bar 4 run into bar 5
tasteNotes.body: Pluck the open G string, hammer on to fret 1, then slap with the open B string. On the high E string, play it open, hammer on to fret 2 with your index finger and to fret 4 with your ring finger. Without picking again, slide the ring finger up to fret 7 for the B4 that starts bar 5. That slide is the first note of the phrase, so let it land right on the knock. Practise the hammer-ons in a loop at 70 bpm before bringing it up to tempo.

tasteNotes.title: Common tones in the reharmonization
tasteNotes.body: C#m7 (x46457) to Amaj7 (x06655) keeps G# on string 4 and E on string 2. Only the bass, the G string and the melody move, so the colour change sounds smooth rather than jumpy. The chromatic B–C–C# bass at the end of bar 6 walks into C#m7. Bring that bass out a little; it is the moment the climax starts.

tasteNotes.title: Melody first, then the groove
tasteNotes.body: Play the melody alone (the top note of each knock or slap beat) until it sings, then add the thumb. The melody is always the highest note when it starts, so if it gets buried, play the inner 8th and 16th notes more softly instead of digging in harder on top.

tasteNotes.title: Reference players
tasteNotes.body: For the knock-and-slap pocket under a simple melody, listen to Sungha Jung's arrangements of children's songs and pop covers. Hear how Kent Nishimura's percussive covers fit harmonics into the gaps in a phrase. Tommy Emmanuel's 'Angelina' shows harmonic chimes used as an ending.

song.title: Jingle Bells — Drop-D Slap & Chime
song.summary: The chorus is moved up a whole step to D and played in drop-D. That puts the melody on the top two strings in first position and lets the open low D act like a kick drum under it. Bars 1–4 set up a pop groove: a body knock on beat 1, a thumb slap on beats 2 and 4, and eighth notes on the inner strings. The harmony is reworked as I–vi–ii9–Vsus4–V–I. Bars 5–8 get busier, with sixteenth notes and a walking D/F# bass. The usual D7 becomes a V9/V chord, which comes out as E9 in this key. The piece ends with a slide up to a 7th-position D chord and a harmonic chime at the 7th fret. Every melody note is kept exactly as written, just transposed up a whole step.

sections.name: A — Groove (bars 1–4)
sections.note: The thumb alternates between the low bass on 1 and 3 and slaps on 2 and 4, while the melody stays on the open-position top strings. Bar 4 is the hook: a 7th-fret harmonic D chord, then a pull-off run down the high E string that leads into bar 5.

sections.name: B — Climax & Chime (bars 5–8)
sections.note: This section is busier: sixteenth-note inner voices, a walking D/F# bass, and an E9 that leans into the turnaround. The ending slides into a 7th-position D chord, then you lighten the same fingers so the strings ring as harmonics.

tasteNotes.title: Where the slap and knock go
tasteNotes.body: Knock the lower bout with your thumb-side palm on beat 1 while your thumb plays the bass. On beats 2 and 4, slap the wound strings with the side of your thumb. Keep the slap as one quick motion with no follow-through, so the treble melody note on that beat (bars 1–2, beat 2) still rings. Never pluck strings 5 or 6 on a slap beat. The bass parts are written to leave those beats free.

tasteNotes.title: The 7th-fret D-chord chime
tasteNotes.body: In drop-D, the 7th-fret natural harmonics on strings 4, 3 and 2 make an A–D–F# triad. That's a full D major chord with no fretting. Lay one finger very lightly across all three strings directly above the fret wire, pick them together, then lift the finger right away. In bar 8 your fingers are already at fret 7 after the slide. Just ease off the pressure and pluck again, and the fretted D turns into the chime.

tasteNotes.title: Bar 4 pull-off cascade
tasteNotes.body: Before beat 4, put your pinky on fret 5, ring finger on fret 3 and middle finger on fret 2, all on the high E string. Slap and pick the fret-5 note at the same moment. Then pull off three times, 5→3→2→0, flicking each finger slightly toward the floor. That gives A–G–F#–E. The open E leads straight into the G melody note on the downbeat of bar 5. Practise it slowly against a metronome so it lands as even sixteenths.

tasteNotes.title: Pop reharmonisation that keeps the melody intact
tasteNotes.body: The original chorus stays mostly on the I chord. Here it becomes I–vi7–ii9–Vsus4–V. D to Bm7 only moves the bass, since the top of the D shape stays put. In the Em9 bar the F# melody becomes the 9th, the bar's D melody note becomes the sus4 of A, and the suspension resolves to C# just as the melody steps to E. The usual D7 in bar 7 is played as E9 here, so the melody's F# is its 9th. That makes the V/V chord sound modern instead of barbershop.

tasteNotes.title: Reference sound
tasteNotes.body: Listen to Sungha Jung's and Kent Nishimura's holiday covers for the kick-and-snare thumb feel. Listen to Tommy Emmanuel's live Christmas medleys for how a melody stays out in front of a busy thumb. Pay attention to how quietly the accompaniment notes are played compared with the melody. That balance matters more than speed.
